doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Future plans and the urge to document veterans
summary: He wants to write more books, laments discarded archives, and values documenting players like Joe Wilder and Jay McShann.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Do you have any immediate goals for future writing coming up?

I always want to do some books you see. I mean that’s the one book I’ve done. I’ve just done a chapter for a rather good book on saxophonists. And I do want to do more of that sort of thing. Because as I was talking the other day, transcribing interviews is the thing that bugs me most. And that remains an issue I have to say.
Yeah. I’m pretty lucky that way.

I know you are. I’m going to come and live in your house. No it’s still this idea that one wants to document. Each time I hear of guy that’s died I think damn, we didn’t get to him. And also I’ve got a very substantial photo archive and I’m kind of always trying to grab the photos, if only to have the chance to copy them. Because otherwise I know they’ll be dished. They’ll be thrown away other than in certain very particular situations. Like Dan Morgenstern was telling us about the Mary Lou Williams Archive which runs to something like 27 boxes of everything. That’s rare. So often you get to someone and they say oh no, we threw all that away. I still have a feeling that we ought to be stopping that, that stuff shouldn’t be thrown away. So I think there’s still that sense that I started out with of wanting to document something. Because the kind of people I’m interested in came out of a time — I was just talking with Joe Wilder — you are talking about a guy who wanted to be a classical trumpet player. He went to the Mastbaum School in Philadelphia which prepared classical trumpet players. But he was black. There was no opportunity. So his experiences are formed by that situation aren’t they? And I think it’s important to document those. Because if you spool forward and you look at Wynton, Wynton was playing the “Hummel Concerto” with the New Orleans Symphony when he was sixteen, wasn’t he? No one said to Wynton you can’t be a classical player because you’re black. And I’m interested still to pursue that documenting of that period, the veteran guys, the best of the lot. But there’s a real story there, when America was sort of in a formative stage. You know when you talk to someone like Jay McShann, as I’m sure you’ve done, you’re talking about a guy that was born in Oklahoma when it wasn’t a state, was it? It was Indian country. And there’s Indian blood in McShann. And just
talking about things like that, it’s another time and it needs to be sort of documented and preserved.
